title: Small jobs, good for the soul
excerpt: Being a great housemate is mostly small jobs done without being asked, and it feels good too.
steps: If you spot a small job, just do it: a full bin, dry dishes, crumbs on the floor.
Post it in the house chat so everyone sees the jobs being shared.
Little and often from everyone keeps the house a nice place to live.
why: Small jobs done by everyone stop resentment building, keep the house clean between cleans, and doing something kind for the people you live with is good for the soul.

title: Kettle on? Put the dry dishes away
excerpt: Use the minute the kettle takes to put the dry dishes away.
steps: While the kettle boils, put away any dry dishes by the sink, whoever’s they are.
Empty the draining rack so it’s ready for the next person.
why: A cleared rack means the next person can wash up straight away, and the kitchen never piles up.

title: Clean as you cook
excerpt: Wash up and wipe down while you cook, and there’s almost nothing left to do afterwards.
steps: While food is cooking, wash the things you’ve finished with.
Wipe up spills on the hob and sides as they happen.
Put ingredients back in the fridge or cupboard as soon as you’ve used them.
why: Grease and food are much easier to clean while they’re fresh, and the kitchen stays usable for everyone.

title: Leave no trace: sink and hob photo
excerpt: After you’ve cooked, leave the kitchen spotless and post a photo of the sink and hob in the house chat.
steps: Wash, dry and put away everything you used.
Wipe the hob, sides and table.
Clear the sink and plughole of food.
Post a quick photo of the clean sink and hob in the house chat.
why: Everyone arrives to a kitchen that’s ready to use, and the photo shows the house is pulling together.

title: Never leave dishes in the sink
excerpt: Dishes left in the sink block it for everyone. Wash them straight after you eat.
steps: Wash your dishes straight after eating, never leave them overnight.
Don’t leave things “soaking” in the sink.
Dry them and put them away.
why: A sink full of someone else’s dishes is the number one cause of falling-outs in shared houses.

title: Your fridge shelf: label it, clear it weekly
excerpt: Keep to your shelf, label your food and clear out anything old each week.
steps: Keep your food on your own shelf, labelled.
Each week, on bin day, throw away anything out of date.
Wipe up spills in the fridge straight away.
Ask before using anyone else’s food.
why: Old food smells, spoils other people’s food and attracts pests.

title: Made a mess? Clean it now
excerpt: Spills and crumbs are yours to clear up straight away. The cleaner is for the regular clean, not everyday mess.
steps: If you spill or drop something, clear it up straight away with the dustpan and brush or a cloth.
Feeling helpful? Give the shared areas a quick hoover between cleans.
Post it in the house chat so everyone knows.
why: Mess left for the cleaner spreads, gets walked through the house and makes the shared rooms unpleasant for everyone.

title: A few minutes’ tidy each day
excerpt: Spend a couple of minutes tidying the shared rooms each day. A little from everyone keeps the house looking great.
steps: Before you leave a shared room, straighten the cushions and clear away your things.
Wipe the table and surfaces you used.
Take cups and plates back to the kitchen.
why: Shared rooms only stay nice if everyone does a little, every day.

title: Your things live in your room
excerpt: Keep your shoes, coats and parcels in your room so shared spaces stay clear for everyone.
steps: Take shoes, coats, bags and parcels to your room.
Don’t store things in the hallway, stairs, kitchen or living room.
Keep the hall and stairs completely clear: it’s your escape route.
why: Clutter in shared areas gets in everyone’s way, and in a fire a clear hallway can save lives.

title: Bin full? Change it and post it
excerpt: When you see a full bin, change it and post it in the house chat. That’s how the informal rota works.
steps: If a bin is full, don’t squash it down or balance more on top: change it.
Tie the bag, take it out to the right outside bin, and put a new liner in.
Post a quick message in the house chat, like “Changed the kitchen bin 👍”.
We keep an eye on these posts so everyone takes a fair turn.
why: The house chat works as an informal rota: everyone can see the bins being shared out, and nobody gets stuck doing it all.

title: Recycling: rinse, flatten, take it out
excerpt: Rinse and flatten recycling, use the right bin, and take it out as soon as it’s full.
steps: Rinse tins and bottles, flatten boxes.
Put each thing in the right bin; food waste goes in its own caddy.
When the recycling or caddy is full, take it out straight away.
Post it in the house chat.
why: Dirty or wrongly sorted recycling smells, attracts pests, and the council may refuse to collect it.

title: Big boxes: cut them down, recycle in stages
excerpt: Got a big delivery? Cut the boxes down and recycle them a bit at a time, so there’s room for everyone’s recycling.
steps: Don’t leave big boxes next to the recycling bins.
Flatten them and cut them into smaller pieces (a bread knife works well).
Put a few pieces neatly inside the recycling bin each collection, so there’s still room for your housemates’ normal recycling.
Never leave cardboard outside the bin.
why: Cardboard left outside gets wet, and wet cardboard can’t be recycled. The council may refuse it, and you could be charged for someone to come and remove it.

title: Weeding the garden
excerpt: Gloves, a black bin bag and half an hour. Then bin one bag a week so the bins never overflow.
steps: Put on gardening gloves and take a black bin bag outside.
Pull the weeds up by the roots and put them straight in the bag.
Tie the bags and keep them neatly out of the way.
Put one bag a week in the general waste bin, so it doesn’t fill up the house’s normal rubbish.
Post it in the house chat: a tidy garden is a job for the whole house.
why: A few bags spread over a few weeks don’t affect the normal household waste. Putting them all out at once fills the bins and blocks everyone’s rubbish.

title: Bin night: out the night before
excerpt: Put the bins out the night before collection and bring them back in once they’re emptied.
steps: Check your bin collection days in the Capital Rooms app.
Put the outside bins out the night before, lids closed.
Bring them back in once they’ve been emptied.
Post it in the house chat so nobody doubles up.
why: A missed collection means overflowing bins for a week or two, which attracts pests and annoys the neighbours.

title: Bathroom: leave it how you’d like to find it
excerpt: Wipe the sink, pick up hair and take your things with you. A clean bathroom is essential in a shared house.
steps: Wipe the sink and remove any hair.
Take your toiletries back to your room, or keep them in your own space.
Open the window or leave the fan on, and close the door.
why: The bathroom is the room everyone shares most closely. Two minutes after each use keeps it fresh for the next person.

title: Shower: hair out, quick squeegee
excerpt: Pick out your hair and squeegee the screen after every shower. It takes ten seconds.
steps: Pick any hair out of the plughole and put it in the bin.
Squeegee or wipe the screen and tiles.
Leave the fan on or the window open, and close the door.
why: Hair blocks drains and water left on screens turns into limescale and mould.

title: Toilet: brush, lid down, new roll
excerpt: Brush, lid down, and never leave an empty roll for the next person.
steps: Use the toilet brush whenever it’s needed.
If you finish the toilet roll, put a new one on and bin the tube.
Put the lid down before flushing.
why: Nobody wants to find a dirty toilet or an empty roll. These are the small things that make sharing easy.

title: Running low? Restock or tell the house
excerpt: Spotted shared supplies running low? Pick some up or post in the house chat before they run out.
steps: Keep an eye on shared basics: washing-up liquid, bin bags, toilet roll, cleaning sprays.
When something is running low, pick some up or post in the house chat.
Take turns restocking so it stays fair.
why: Running out of bin bags or toilet roll is how small annoyances start. A quick message keeps everything stocked.
